https://timesofindia.indiatimes.com/worl.text: Ukraine unleashed a barrage of drones towards Moscow and other parts of Russia early Sunday, one of its biggest aerial attacks since Russia's full-scale invasion began. The assault killed at least six people and damaged various infrastructure, including civilian residences and a Wildberries warehouse.The scale of the attack was captured in dramatic visuals from across the Moscow region, with explosions lighting up the night sky, plumes of smoke rising over the capital and fires breaking out at several locations.Russian authorities said the country's air defences intercepted hundreds of Ukrainian drones, including a large number heading towards Moscow.Russia's ministry of defence said it had destroyed 822 Ukrainian drones overnight, while Moscow Mayor Sergei Sobyanin said around 600 drones were detected heading towards the Russian capital. About a third of those were destroyed over the Moscow region itself.The attack killed an 83-year-old man after a Ukrainian drone struck a private home in the Moscow region, regional governor Andrey Vorobyov said. He also confirmed that another Ukrainian strike triggered a fire at a Wildberries warehouse in Podolsk, adding to a growing pattern of attacks on the Russian online retailer's facilities.In Russia's southwestern Rostov region, five people were killed after more than 150 drones targeted three towns, regional governor Yury Slyusar said. Several homes and a railway station were damaged, while a forest fire was also reported.The latest barrage reflects Kyiv's increasingly aggressive use of long-range weapons against targets deep inside Russia. Ukrainian forces have intensified drone and missile attacks this year, focusing on military-industrial facilities, energy infrastructure and other sites linked to Russia's war effort.The attacks have also increasingly reached areas familiar to ordinary Russians. Wildberries warehouses have repeatedly been targeted, with previous strikes destroying merchandise worth billions of dollars and bringing the consequences of the war closer to the civilian population nearly four and a half years after Moscow launched its full-scale invasion.Russian strikes hit UkraineAs Russia came under one of the largest Ukrainian aerial assaults of the war, Ukraine itself faced another wave of Russian strikes.A Russian missile attack on Kryvyi Rih killed two people and wounded 14 others, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on Sunday. One more person was killed in Sumy, he added.In the southern Zaporizhzhia region, a man and a woman were killed after a Russian strike hit their home, according to Ivan Fedorov, head of the regional military administration.Russian attacks also caused fires across Kyiv, injuring six people. Among the most striking scenes was a major blaze at one of the capital's largest book markets near the Pochaina metro station.Footage from the scene showed flames tearing through tightly packed market kiosks, with thick black smoke spreading across the city. Firefighters battled the blaze as parts of the market were reduced to rubble.âWherever the Russians can reach with their ballistic missiles, they strike civilian infrastructure,â Zelenskyy said.Russia's Defence Ministry said its forces had targeted a metallurgical plant in Kryvyi Rih and several military-industrial facilities in Kyiv, including a manufacturing facility for Ukraine's domestically produced Flamingo missiles.The missiles have become an increasingly important component of Ukraine's long-range strike capability. Zelenskyy said on Saturday that Kyiv had used Flamingo missiles to attack a rocket research and production centre in Samara, about 900 kilometres (560 miles) from the Ukrainian border.Drone enters NATO airspaceThe escalation also spilled beyond the immediate battlefield, with Romania reporting that a drone had entered its airspace before being shot down by a Spanish fighter jet.Romania's Ministry of National Defence said the drone was detected at 4:44 am, around 24 kilometres (14.9 miles) north of the eastern city of Galati, close to the border with Moldova.A Spanish Air and Space Force F-18, deployed for air-policing duties, established radar contact with the drone and received authorisation to engage.âThe drone was safely shot down by the F-18 aircraft at 05:01,â the ministry said.Debris from the drone was later reported in the Black Sea at around 10 am, approximately 1.5 kilometres (0.9 miles) from the coastal city of Constanta.Romanian officials did not identify the origin of the drone.The incident comes after a series of similar episodes along Romania's border with Ukraine. Romanian pilots shot down three drones over three days in recent weeks as Russian attacks intensified in areas close to the NATO member's territory.Since Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine, Romania has reported dozens of drone-related incidents, including cases in which drones crashed and exploded on Romanian soil.Acting Foreign Minister Oana Toiu said on X that Spain's deployment had been expanded âat the request of Romania and NATO to bolster the Eastern Flank following prior drone incidents,â adding that it was Spain's fourth such deployment.The latest attacks underline how the war is increasingly being fought beyond the front lines, with Ukrainian strikes reaching deep into Russia while Russian bombardments continue to hit Ukrainian cities and civilian infrastructure. The entry of a drone into NATO airspace also highlights the growing risk of the conflict spilling beyond Ukraine's borders. Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

https://www.dw.com/en/japan-typhoon-duju.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5MwY1 The Japan Meteorological Agency (JMA) has issued evacuation advisories for some parts Image: Kyodo/REUTERS Advertisement A powerful typhoon was nearing Japan 's eastern coast on Monday, triggering flood and landslide warnings, evacuation advisories and prompting hundreds of flights to be canceled. The Japan Meteorological Agency issued level 5 emergency warning for the Izu islands, with the advisory cautioning a "life-threatening situation" and for residents to "ensure safety immediately." A level 5 warning is the highest level of alert on the agency's scale. Dujuan is forecast to pass close to the Tokyo metropolitan area later in the day and than one million people have been reported to be under evacuation advisories. The typhoon's wind speeds were at 144 kilometres (89 miles) per hour as the storm was approximately 110 kilometres from Hachijojima Image: CSU/CIRA AND KMA/NMSC/Handout/REUTERS What do we know about Typhoon Dujuan? Typhoon Dujuan was packing winds at speeds of 144 kilometers (89 miles) per hour as it lingered some 110 kilometres from Hachijojima, one of Tokyo's most remote islands. Parts of the Izu Islands and the Chiba prefecture near Tokyo already saw heavy rainfall over the weekend. The ⁠Japan Meteorological Agency (JMA) has cautioned that weather conditions could worsen rapidly. "The total rainfall through Tuesday could exceed the average monthly rainfall for September, resulting in record-breaking heavy rain," the JMA said. Authorities have also warned of a possibility of ⁠linear ​rain bands forming over central Japan and the Kanto region — which includes Tokyo and surrounding prefectures — that could raise the risk of rain-related disasters like flash floods and landslides. Linear ‌bands cause heavy torrential rainfall ​over a narrow area for several hours. Dujuan is Japan's 25th typhoon of the year Image: Ichiro Ohara/AP Photo/picture alliance How have Japan's regions been affected by the incoming storm? Over 4,000 households in Chiba were without power. In the central prefecture of Aichi, which is currently hosting the Asian Games, an equestrian eventing competition was postponed until Tuesday. The Tokyo Game Show, one of the world's biggest video game trade fairs, was shut down ahead of its final day on Monday. Dujuan could also scupper travel plans during Japan's "Silver Week" holiday, which has just begun and which normally sees a surge in domestic travel. On Monday, Japan Airlines canceled 120 domestic and 15 international flights, while All Nippon Airways canceled 140 domestic flights. Some railway services were suspended on some lines in Tokyo and its neighboring areas. https://www.thenews.com.pk/latest/141699.text: Russia could test NATO in coming months, European intelligence chiefs warn Michal Koudelka, head of the Czech Republic’s BIS security service says that possible Russian actions could include increased drone activity European intelligence officials have warned that Russia could escalate its actions against NATO countries in the coming months, although Baltic security chiefs say there is no evidence of an imminent attack. Michal Koudelka, head of the Czech Republic’s BIS security service, told The Guardian that possible Russian actions could include increased drone activity, false flag operations or a limited incursion into NATO territory. “It’s possible. It could involve a limited incursion, false flag provocations, a massive influence campaign,” Koudelka said, adding such a scenario could emerge within “months, not years”. However, Latvia’s state security chief Normunds Mežviets urged caution: “We don’t see indications of an imminent attack,” he told the Guardian. He said there were signs Moscow was preparing for more decisive action in Europe, but it remained unclear whether this represented concrete military planning or an effort to create fear and uncertainty. The warnings follow Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk’s statement that intelligence assessments suggest Russia could use drones or missiles against NATO territory in the coming months. Russia has denied plans to attack NATO as a Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov previously said such claims had “nothing to do with reality and nothing to do with the intentions of the Russian Federation”. Photograph: I-Hwa Cheng/AFP/Getty Images Taiwan Typhoon Champi kills one and injures more than 500 in Taiwan as it heads to China Super typhoon weakening but large parts of Taiwan, including Taipei, still mostly closed and flights cancelled Reuters Fri 23 Oct 2026 22.22 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Typhoon Champi swept past Taiwan on Saturday killing one person, injuring more than 500, and uprooting trees and severing power as it weakened and ⁠headed north toward ⁠the ​Chinese coast. Earlier classified as a super typhoon and one of the strongest storms in the ⁠Pacific this year, Champi was still packing gusts of about 126km per hour (78 miles per hour) near its ⁠centre, according to Taiwan’s Central Weather Administration (CWA). The storm was about ​150km (93 miles) east ‌of Taiwan, the CWA ‌said, having glanced off the island’s northeast coast in the early ‌hours of Saturday. Champi’s forecast track shows it turning north toward the Chinese coast before eventually moving into southern Japan . View image in fullscreen Waves generated by Typhoon Champi crash against a seawall in Keelung. Photograph: Ann Wang/Reuters Taiwan’s fire department said one man had been killed, swept by waves from the ‌island of Liuqiu. Another 527 people were injured during heavy wind and torrential rain. Taipower said more than 167,000 homes had lost electricity, but most had now been reconnected. Large parts of northern and central Taiwan, including Taipei, declared a second ​day of ‌office and ​school closures ​on Saturday, and some flights were still being cancelled. Taiwan is generally well prepared for typhoons, which keeps casualties low. Although more common in summer, the storms can strike also in autumn. Nearly half a million Russian soldiers may have been killed in Vladimir Putin 's war in Ukraine. Can Russia continue fighting at such an enormous human and economic cost? Leaked records reportedly obtained from Russia's state statistics agency, Rosstat, identify more than 412,000 deaths linked to the war. British newspaper The Guardian reports that the true death toll could be closer to 500,000. The full dataset has not been independently verified. Some months saw more than 500 Russian soldiers killed every day. And the losses have fallen disproportionately on Russia's poorer and more remote regions. In this DW News interview, Janis Kluge, head of the Eastern Europe and Eurasia research division at the German Institute for International and Security Affairs (SWP), examines what the leaked figures reveal about Russia's military losses, recruitment crisis and war economy. The leaked data comes as US-mediated peace talks between Russia and Ukraine conclude in Abu Dhabi without a breakthrough on ending the war. The two sides have agreed to a prisoner exchange, but fundamental disagreements remain. Could mounting Russian losses eventually force Putin to compromise, or make him even more determined to continue the war?
